text: On the twenty fourth of September, the Madhya Pradesh High Court ordered the state to renew all of Som Distilleries' manufacturing licences within fifteen days.
The Bhopal brewery had been shut since February. And the company's own filings show what that licence was worth: about half its volume, half its quarterly income, and its investment grade rating.
This is the story of seven months, told only from the company's own filings.
Chapter one. Seven months, in the company's filings.
On the fifth of February, Madhya Pradesh's Excise Commissioner suspended the Bhopal manufacturing licence.

The suspension was tied to a case from twenty twelve. The company said it was not a party to it. The judgment related to individuals who, it said, were not its employees at the time, and the High Court at Indore had stayed their sentences on appeal.
On the second of June, management said Bhopal supplied roughly half of its volume, and assumed the plant would restart that month.
It did not. On the eighteenth and nineteenth of June, the licence application for the new financial year was rejected.
The ratings followed. On the twenty seventh of June, Infomerics cut the company to triple B, from triple B plus. On the thirtieth, ICRA cut two subsidiaries to triple B minus, from triple B.
And on the twentieth of August, Infomerics cut the company again, to double B plus. That is below investment grade.
Chapter two. What the licence was worth.
The best measure is the quarter the plant was shut for the whole three months: the June quarter of this financial year.
Total income fell to two hundred and sixty eight point eight crore rupees, from five hundred and thirty point one crore a year earlier.
EBITDA fell to fifteen point two crore, from seventy two point one. Profit after tax fell to one point six crore, from forty two point one. Volume was down forty eight percent.
Asked on the call how much revenue the closure cost, management answered: I think we lost about two hundred and fifty crores of revenue.
It also said the idle plant still costs close to six to seven crores a quarter, in interest, salaries and electricity. About twenty five crore rupees of finished goods sat in the plant.

Bhopal is the company's largest brewery. Fifteen point two million cases a year of beer capacity, against fourteen million at Hassan, nine million in Odisha, and ten million at the new Uttar Pradesh plant.
Chapter three. Why the other plants could not fill the gap.
The obvious question is why the company did not supply Madhya Pradesh from its other breweries. It did look at it.

Management said the cost of bringing beer in from another state is exorbitant, and it will erode our margins. Not even erode, it will be at a loss, particularly because of the import fee, very huge import fees that Madhya Pradesh has.
That answer holds the whole economics of Indian alcohol. Each state controls who may make, move and sell alcohol inside it, and charges heavily to bring it in from outside.
A licensed local plant is a real advantage. And it can be switched off by one state order.
Chapter four. What held up.

Management said the Hassan plant ran at about sixty percent utilisation in the quarter, and Odisha at about seventy percent, with case sales up about thirty percent in Karnataka and close to forty percent in Odisha.

The new Uttar Pradesh brewery, which cost about three hundred crore rupees, started commercial production in the quarter without new external debt. Gross debt to equity was zero point three one times at June.
And on the fifth of September, the board approved issuing warrants worth about twenty five crore rupees, at seventy seven rupees and eighty one paise each, to promoter Deepak Arora.
Chapter five. The bear case, taken seriously.
One. An order to renew is not a running plant. The court gave fifteen days, to around the ninth of October. None of the filings read says when production will actually restart.
Two. The state may not be finished. The filings do not say whether the government will appeal.
Three. Lost drinkers may not return quickly. An investor on the August call made exactly this point. Management agreed: it is a long haul. It is not easy.
Four. The ratings are still below investment grade. Infomerics' double B plus was assigned in August.
Five. The same exposure remains. Karnataka and Odisha carry the business today, on the same kind of licence that Bhopal lost.
Chapter six. Why it matters, and what to watch.
In a state licensed industry, the licence is the moat, and also the biggest single risk. The court order restores the first. It does not remove the second.
Watch four things. The actual renewal, due around the ninth of October. The first quarter with Bhopal running again. Any appeal by the state. And whether the ratings recover.
And keep one number in mind. The June guidance of about fourteen hundred crore rupees of sales assumed nine months of Bhopal operating. That time has already been lost.
Every fact in this video comes from Som Distilleries' own filings, investor presentation and earnings call transcripts. The links are in the description.
